title: Indian-American Couple Gives $4 Million to University of Houston Engineering College
excerpt: Manmohan Singh Kalsi and Marie-Luise Schubert Kalsi's gift to UH's Cullen College of Engineering funds professorships, fellowships and a seminar series, marking one of the largest donations to the mechanical engineering department in recent years.
body:
• Manmohan Singh Kalsi and Marie-Luise Schubert Kalsi have committed $4 million to the University of Houston's Cullen College of Engineering.
  • The gift establishes two endowed professorships, the Kalsi Faculty Research Fund, graduate fellowships and the Kalsi Seminar Series in the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering.
  • Kalsi earned his master's and Ph.D. in mechanical engineering from UH and founded Kalsi Engineering in 1978, a firm known for sealing and valve technology used in nuclear power plants.
  • The gift advances UH's "Can't Stop Houston" centennial campaign and its drive to rank among the top 50 public universities in the United States.

A prominent Indian-American couple has committed $4 million to the University of Houston's Cullen College of Engineering, in one of the largest philanthropic donations to the college's Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering in recent years. The gift, from Manmohan Singh Kalsi and Marie-Luise Schubert Kalsi, was announced by the university on September 4, 2026, and will support faculty, graduate research and industry engagement across the department.

The commitment creates both endowed and current-use funds. Two endowed professorships are intended to help the department attract and retain leading faculty; the Kalsi Faculty Research Fund will advance emerging research; and endowed and current-use fellowships will recruit outstanding graduate students. A new Kalsi Seminar Series will bring internationally recognized researchers and industry leaders to campus, according to the university.

A half-century relationship with UH

For Manmohan Kalsi, the gift is a return to the institution that launched his career. Kalsi earned his bachelor's degree in mechanical engineering from Punjab Engineering College in India in 1967, then came to the United States for graduate study at the University of Houston, earning his master's in 1970 and his Ph.D. in 1975 while working full-time in industry.

After a decade in valve design and manufacturing, Kalsi founded Kalsi Engineering in Houston in 1978. The company, recognized worldwide for solving valve and sealing problems in the oilfield, petrochemical and nuclear power industries, pioneered hydrodynamic rotary sealing technology used to ensure the safety and reliability of nuclear power plants. Nearly five decades later, the firm continues to employ UH graduates.

Kalsi has credited the late UH professor Gabriel Fazekas with shaping his trajectory; in 2014, the couple established an endowed professorship at the Cullen College in Fazekas's honor. The new gift extends that longstanding support.

"This gift will help us to recruit and retain world-class faculty while providing our graduate students the financial support and research infrastructure needed to solve real-world challenges."

— Pradeep Sharma, Dean, Cullen College of Engineering

Karolos Grigoriadis, chair of the Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, said the gift "provides a tremendous boost to our department's strategic momentum," strengthening "every part of our research enterprise" from faculty to graduate researchers to collaborative seminars.

A distinct chapter in Texas philanthropy

The $4 million commitment is distinct from another recent large Indian-origin gift in Texas — a separate $20 million donation from a different couple to establish an AI college at the University of North Texas. Together, the gifts point to a growing pattern of major diaspora philanthropy directed at Texas public universities.

University officials framed the Kalsi gift as part of UH's "Can't Stop Houston: The Centennial Campaign," the comprehensive fundraising initiative to launch the university's second century by investing in innovation, student success and campus transformation. Russell T. Dunlavy, vice president for advancement and alumni, said the Kalsis "exemplify the enduring impact of a University of Houston education," noting that the success of Kalsi Engineering "grew from the talent, mentorship and spirit of innovation that define this University."

Why it matters for Houston's Indian-American community

Houston is home to one of the largest Indian-American communities in the United States, and the gift resonates with a familiar immigrant trajectory: arriving for graduate study, building a company over decades, and endowing the institution that provided the foothold. Kalsi's path — night-school-era graduate work, mentorship from a single professor, and an enterprise that became a global standard in its niche — is the kind of story the region's diaspora entrepreneurs cite often.

For Indian-American students and families weighing engineering careers in Texas, the gift also has practical implications: endowed professorships and fellowships expand the financial infrastructure of a department that feeds directly into Houston's energy, aerospace and manufacturing industries.

What's next

The university says the professorships, research fund, fellowships and seminar series will be stood up through the current campaign cycle. Watch for the appointment of the two endowed professors and the first Kalsi Seminar Series speakers, and for further large diaspora gifts as UH pushes toward its top-50 public university goal.
